findings.title: Periodic connections: 10.0.19.14 → 10.0.19.9:445 (32 connections, ~724.4s interval)
findings.description: 10.0.19.14 connected to 10.0.19.9:445 32 times with a mean interval of 724.4s and low timing variance (CV=0.39).
findings.explanation: Malware check-ins are often timer-driven, so their connection intervals are far more regular than human-driven traffic. BUT: software updaters, NTP clients, monitoring agents and messaging apps also produce regular traffic. This is an indicator to investigate, not evidence of compromise on its own. Check the destination's reputation and the stream content.
findings.verification: In Wireshark: ip.addr == 10.0.19.9 && tcp.port == 445 — look at the time column (Δtime) between connections.
evidence: payload size uniformity: CV 0.56 across 32 data-bearing connections

mitre.name: Non-Application Layer Protocol
mitre.why: regularly-timed repeated connections consistent with a C2 check-in schedule

findings.title: Possible covert-channel candidate: http Host header of 10.0.19.14
findings.description: The Host header field across 18 HTTP messages from 10.0.19.14 varies over a small alphabet (ctldl.windowsupdate.com, x1.c.lencr.org, oceriesfornot.top, r3.i.lencr.org) in a low-cardinality (4-state) repeated sequence. Mapping the values to bits and grouping 8 per byte yields 4 bytes that decode to printable-looking output (100%).
findings.explanation: Protocol metadata fields that the sender can freely choose (HTTP version, query type, TTL, port…) can carry hidden information by *value selection*: every packet is legal on its own, and only the sequence encodes data. This is an indicator, not proof — the same variation can occur naturally (client pools, load balancers). Judge by whether the decoded output is meaningful and whether the pattern persists. Full derivation: `netsleuth covert <pcap>`.
findings.verification: In Wireshark: http.host && ip.src == 10.0.19.14 — read the field of each packet in order, note the values (the engine observed: oceriesfornot.top×1, ctldl.windowsupdate.com×12, r3.i.lencr.org×1, x1.c.lencr.org×4), assign bits per the mapping and decode 8 bits per byte.

mitre.name: Data Encoding: Standard Encoding
mitre.why: information encoded into protocol field choices rather than payload

mitre.name: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
mitre.why: application/protocol metadata used as a covert data channel

findings.title: ICMP echo requests carrying 32 bytes of data payload
findings.description: 1 echo request(s) carry payloads of 32+ bytes (normal ping payloads are usually small and uniform).
findings.explanation: The ping protocol has no business carrying rich text/binary data. Large or varied payloads inside ICMP echo are how simple backdoors exfiltrate or beacon while slipping past port-based rules. Some monitoring tools do embed data, so read the payload before judging.
findings.verification: In Wireshark: icmp && data.len >= 16, then inspect the echo data field.

mitre.name: Non-Application Layer Protocol
mitre.why: ICMP echo used as a data channel

mitre.name: Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol
mitre.why: data moved over an unencrypted non-application protocol

findings.title: High NXDOMAIN rate for burnincandle.com (43/64)
findings.description: 43 of 64 queries under burnincandle.com returned NXDOMAIN (domain does not exist).
findings.explanation: Bursts of NXDOMAIN usually mean one of: a DGA (malware generating random domains to find its C2), subdomain brute-forcing, or simply broken software retrying a hard-coded name. On its own this is weak — correlate with the querying host's other activity.

mitre.name: Application Layer Protocol: DNS
mitre.why: high-volume failing DNS lookups (DGA-style behavior)

findings.title: Possible DNS tunneling via burnincandle.com
findings.description: 64 queries to *.burnincandle.com show high-entropy labels (max 3.729 bits/char — consistent with encoded data, not words).
findings.explanation: DNS tunneling encodes data (C2 commands or exfiltrated bytes) into hostname labels — e.g. NBSWY3DPFQQFO33SNRSC65LJMQ.tunnel.example.com. The encoding forces long, high-entropy, ever-changing subdomains, which is what these signals measure. Legitimate services (CDNs, load balancers) can also generate many subdomains — check whether the labels decode to something meaningful before calling it malicious.
findings.verification: In Wireshark: dns.qry.name contains "burnincandle.com" — inspect the queried names; try Base32/Base64-decoding the left-most label of the longest ones.

mitre.name: Application Layer Protocol: DNS
mitre.why: DNS used as a data channel

mitre.name: Data Encoding: Standard Encoding
mitre.why: hostname labels consistent with encoded data
